topics: Partial fractions (proper, improper, repeated, quadratic denominator)

body.en: Polynomial division and partial fractions break complicated algebraic fractions into simpler pieces.
A proper fraction \( \tfrac{px+q}{(x+a)(x+b)} \) splits as \( \tfrac{A}{x+a}+\tfrac{B}{x+b} \). If the fraction is improper, divide first.

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Algebra: Partial Fractions & Division

body.en:
Structural Decomposition Theorem: Any proper rational expression \(\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) with \(\deg P < \deg Q\) over \(\mathbb{R}\) decomposes uniquely into a sum of simpler fractions determined by the factorization of \(Q(x)\). When \(\deg P \ge \deg Q\), Euclidean polynomial division yields \(\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = Q_{\text{quot}}(x) + \dfrac{R(x)}{Q(x)}\) with \(\deg R < \deg Q\).

For distinct linear factors \((x - a_1)(x - a_2)\), Heaviside's cover-up rule gives the exact residue \(A_k = \lim_{x \to a_k} (x - a_k)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\). For a repeated factor \((x - a)^m\), all intermediate powers \((x - a)^1, (x - a)^2, \dots, (x - a)^m\) must be included to span the full \(m\)-dimensional rational subspace.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Algebra: Partial Fractions & Division)

body.en:
Why Heaviside Cover-Up & Repeated-Factor Forms Work: Consider \(\dfrac{px + q}{(x - 5)(x + 5)} \equiv \dfrac{A}{x - 5} + \dfrac{B}{x + 5}\). Multiplying both sides by \((x - 5)(x + 5)\) yields the polynomial identity:

\[ px + q \equiv A(x + 5) + B(x - 5) \]

Because two polynomials equal on \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{5, -5\}\) must be equal for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) by continuity, setting \(x = 5\) annihilates the \(B\) term and isolates \(A = \dfrac{5p + q}{10}\). For a repeated root \((x - a)^2\), writing only \(\dfrac{B}{(x - a)^2}\) restricts the numerator to a constant \(B\), which cannot match a general linear numerator \(px + q\); adding \(\dfrac{A}{x - a}\) supplies \(A(x - a) + B\), spanning all degree-1 numerators.

Express \(\dfrac{x^3+2x}{x^2-1}\) in partial fractions (after division).

Degree of numerator ≥ denominator, so divide first: \(x^3+2x=(x^2-1)\cdot x+3x\). So:

\[\frac{x^3+2x}{x^2-1}=x+\frac{3x}{(x-1)(x+1)}=x+\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+1}.\]

Cover-up: \(A=\tfrac{3}{2}\), \(B=\tfrac{3}{2}\). Result: \(x+\dfrac{3/2}{x-1}+\dfrac{3/2}{x+1}\).

label.en: Worked Example C — Algebra: Partial Fractions & Division (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): Find the remainder when \( P(x)=-4x^{3}-x^{2}-3x+1 \) is divided by \( (x-2) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: By the Remainder Theorem: remainder \( =P(2)=-41 \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Algebra: Partial Fractions & Division (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): Find the constant term of the quotient when \( 6x^{2}-3x+9 \) is divided by \( (x-2) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Dividing: quotient \( =6x+9 \), remainder \( =27 \). Constant term of quotient: 9.

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Algebra: Partial Fractions & Division)

rows.en: Right-hand side has degree \(-1\) as \(x \to \infty\), whereas LHS approaches \(1\).
Two identical denominators merge into a single fraction, leaving an underdetermined system.
Include every power up to multiplicity: \(\tfrac{A}{x-5} + \tfrac{B}{(x-5)^2}\).
Using \(\tfrac{B}{x^2+5}\) for an irreducible quadratic factor
Fails to account for the \(x\)-term remainder when dividing by a degree-2 factor.
Always use a degree-1 numerator: \(\tfrac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 5}\).

body.en: 10-Second Sanity Check on Cambridge International A Level (9709 Paper 3 / Paper 6): After finding \(A, B, C\), substitute \(x = 0\) (or \(x = 2\)) into both the original rational expression and your partial-fraction sum. If the two numerical fractions do not match, re-check your sign when subtracting negative roots.

label.en: ⚠️ Cambridge 9709 Traps — Improper Fractions & Repeated Factor Forms

body.en:
Checking the Degree First: Before setting up partial fractions, always inspect the degrees: \(\deg(\text{numerator})\) vs \(\deg(\text{denominator})\). If the degree of the top is greater than or equal to the bottom, the fraction is improper. You MUST perform algebraic long division first. Setting up partial fractions directly without dividing will yield impossible equations or wrong coefficients.

Repeated Linear Factors: For a denominator with a repeated term like \((x-1)^2(x+2)\), the correct template is:

\[\frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{(x-1)^2} + \frac{C}{x+2}\]

Omitting the single power \(\frac{A}{x-1}\) is an immediate error that invalidates the rest of the problem.

solution.en:
Set up the partial fraction decomposition with repeated linear factor:

\[\frac{x^2 + 7x - 6}{(x-1)^2(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{(x-1)^2} + \frac{C}{x+2}\]

Multiply both sides by \((x-1)^2(x+2)\):

\[x^2 + 7x - 6 = A(x-1)(x+2) + B(x+2) + C(x-1)^2\]

Substitute \(x = 1\):

\[1 + 7 - 6 = B(3) \implies 2 = 3B \implies B = \frac{2}{3}\]

Substitute \(x = -2\):

\[4 - 14 - 6 = C(-3)^2 \implies -16 = 9C \implies C = -\frac{16}{9}\]

Equate coefficients of \(x^2\):

\[1 = A + C \implies A = 1 - \left(-\frac{16}{9}\right) = \frac{25}{9}\]

Final partial fractions:

\[\frac{25/9}{x-1} + \frac{2/3}{(x-1)^2} - \frac{16/9}{x+2}\]

question.en: [Practice 3 · Hard] Given that \( (x-4) \) is a factor of \( P(x)=3x^{3}-7x^{2}-x+m \), find the value of \( m \).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Algebra: Partial Fractions & Division and start from \( (x-4) \).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( P(4)=0 \Rightarrow 76+m=0\Rightarrow m=-76 \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: By the Factor Theorem: \( P(4)=0 \Rightarrow 76+m=0\Rightarrow m=-76 \).

solution.en: By the Factor Theorem: \( P(-4)=0 \Rightarrow -88+m=0\Rightarrow m=88 \).
